Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

- Key findings and impressions (transcript + DDx consistent):  
  - Young woman with 2 days of constant suprapubic ache and nausea, increased urinary frequency, and recent pink-tinged urine/spotting. Uses Implanon implant; sexually active. Recent constipation has resolved. Subjective feverishness. No dysuria, no vaginal discharge, no vomiting, no light-headedness.

- Differential diagnoses consistent with transcript and DDx:  
  1) Pregnancy-related pathology (including threatened miscarriage or ectopic) — High likelihood: supported by intermenstrual spotting and pelvic pain; clinician prioritized ruling out pregnancy.  
  2) Urinary tract infection / acute cystitis with possible haematuria — Moderate–High likelihood: supported by suprapubic ache, increased urinary frequency, and pink urine; absence of dysuria does not exclude UTI.  
  3) Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) — Moderate likelihood: supported by lower abdominal pain and spotting; lower likelihood given absence of discharge and single regular partner.  
  4) Post-constipation or functional bowel pain — Moderate likelihood: prior constipation could explain some suprapubic discomfort but does not explain spotting/pink urine well.

- Working diagnosis and management priorities:  
  - Working priority: Exclude pregnancy (including ectopic) as urgent first step.  
  - Concurrent priorities: Evaluate for UTI (urine dip/culture) and assess for PID or other gynecological pathology with pelvic examination; consider imaging if indicated after clinical assessment.  
  - Safety priority: escalate if worsening pain, syncope/light-headedness, heavy bleeding, or systemic deterioration.

Management Plan

- Immediate management actions and recommendations documented:  
  - Arrange urgent face-to-face GP appointment today for physical examination, pregnancy test, and further investigations.  
  - Recommend urine dipstick and possible urine culture at face-to-face visit to assess for haematuria/UTI.  
  - Recommend pelvic examination and pregnancy test to exclude ectopic or miscarriage; consider pelvic ultrasound if clinical concern persists or pregnancy test positive.  
  - Advise patient to seek urgent medical attention if symptoms worsen (develop light-headedness, fainting, severe abdominal pain, heavy vaginal bleeding, high fever).  
  - Note allergy: Amoxicillin allergy documented; avoid prescribing amoxicillin.  
  - No medications prescribed during this consultation.

- Follow-up and patient education:  
  - Patient advised clinician will see in person; instructed to present urgently if deteriorates.  
  - Education provided regarding need to rule out pregnancy and possible causes (UTI, PID, gynecological causes).

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)

- 1) Pregnancy-related pathology (threatened miscarriage or ectopic pregnancy) — High likelihood  
  - Justification: Intermenstrual spotting/pink-tinged urine with lower abdominal pain and nausea; clinician explicitly recommended pregnancy testing.  
- 2) Urinary tract infection (acute cystitis) with possible haematuria — Moderate–High likelihood  
  - Justification: Increased urinary frequency, suprapubic ache, and pink urine suggest cystitis/haematuria; absence of dysuria reduces classic presentation but does not exclude.  
- 3) Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) — Moderate likelihood  
  - Justification: Lower abdominal pain and intermenstrual bleeding are compatible; lack of vaginal discharge and single regular partner make PID less likely than other causes.
